summary: Signs, traffic signals, and lines on the pavement all tell you how to drive before you reach a hazard. This chapter covers the three families of signs (regulatory, warning, and guide), what steady and flashing lights and arrows mean, and how to read yellow and white lines on the road.

Shape and color tell you a lot even before you can read the words. The red eight-sided sign always means stop, and the red and white triangle pointing down always means yield. Warning signs are usually yellow diamonds with black words or symbols, and work zone signs are orange. The pennant-shaped sign on the left side of the road marks the start of a no passing zone, and the five-sided sign means you are coming to a school zone.

Traffic signals work the same way every time. A flashing red light means the same as a stop sign, and a flashing yellow light means slow down and go with care. A green arrow gives you a protected turn, while a flashing yellow arrow lets you turn only after you yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.

Pavement markings finish the picture. Yellow lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions, and white lines separate lanes moving the same way. You may pass when a broken yellow line is on your side, but never across a solid yellow line on your side or across a double solid yellow line.

concepts.definition: A red eight-sided sign means come to a full stop and go only when it is safe. A red and white triangle pointing down means slow down and give the right of way to traffic and pedestrians, stopping if you need to.
concepts.tip: Eight sides: stop all the way. Triangle pointing down: give way.

concepts.definition: Warning signs are usually diamond shaped with black words or symbols on a yellow background. They warn of hazards ahead, such as curves, merging traffic, or a traffic signal ahead. Work zone signs are normally diamond shaped too, but orange with black lettering.
concepts.tip: Yellow diamond: hazard ahead. Orange: road work.

concepts.definition: The only pennant-shaped warning sign. It is yellow, is placed on the left side of the road facing the driver, and marks the beginning of a no passing zone.
concepts.tip: Pennant on the left, where you would look before passing.

concepts.definition: The only five-sided (pentagon) sign on the road. It means you are approaching a school zone. Its background may be yellow or fluorescent yellow-green.
concepts.tip: Five sides, like the outline of a schoolhouse.

concepts.definition: A round yellow sign with an X and two R letters warns that a railroad crossing is ahead. At the tracks, the white X-shaped crossbuck sign should be treated like a yield sign: slow down and be ready to stop if a train is coming.
concepts.tip: Round sign: railroad ahead. X-shaped crossbuck: you are at the tracks.

concepts.definition: A flashing red light means the same as a stop sign: stop completely and go only when the intersection is clear. A flashing yellow light means slow down and proceed with care. A green arrow gives a protected turn. A flashing yellow arrow allows a turn only after you yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians. A steady yellow arrow means the turn signal is about to turn red.
concepts.tip: Flashing red acts like a stop sign. Flashing yellow means caution.

concepts.definition: Yellow lines separate traffic going in opposite directions. White lines separate lanes going in the same direction. A broken line may be crossed to pass when it is safe; a solid line on your side may not be crossed to pass. A double solid yellow line means no passing in either direction.
concepts.tip: Yellow means oncoming traffic is on the other side of the line.

points: An eight-sided red sign means stop. A downward-pointing triangle means yield.
The pennant-shaped NO PASSING ZONE sign is on the left side of the road.
The five-sided sign means a school zone is ahead.
A flashing red light means the same as a STOP sign.
A flashing yellow arrow allows a turn only after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.
A double solid yellow line means no passing in either direction.

summary: Right of way rules decide who goes first when two road users want the same space. This chapter covers stop signs and four-way stops, turns on red, roundabouts, and the times when you must stop or yield for pedestrians, emergency vehicles, school buses, and trains.

At a four-way stop every vehicle must stop. The first vehicle to reach the intersection goes first. If two vehicles arrive at the same time, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right. You may turn right on a red light after a full stop unless a sign forbids it, but you must yield to pedestrians and cross traffic first. When you enter a roundabout, yield to the vehicles already in the circle.

Some vehicles always get the right of way. When you hear a siren or see flashing red or red and blue lights from an emergency vehicle, pull over to the curb or side of the road and stop, staying clear of intersections. When a school bus has its red lights flashing and its stop arm out, stop at least 10 feet away. The only exception is when you are on the opposite side of a divided highway with a physical barrier such as a median or guide rail.

At railroad crossings, treat the crossbuck sign like a yield sign. Stop for flashing red lights, a lowered gate, a flagger, or a train's horn, and never drive around a gate. If traffic is backed up, stop where your vehicle is fully clear of the tracks.

concepts.definition: Traffic from all directions must stop. The first vehicle to arrive goes first. If two vehicles arrive at the same time, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right.
concepts.tip: First come, first served. A tie goes to the driver on the right.

concepts.definition: After coming to a full stop, you may turn right at a red light when traffic is clear, unless a sign prohibits it. You must yield to pedestrians and cross traffic.
concepts.tip: Stop first, look, then turn only if no sign says NO TURN ON RED.

concepts.definition: A circular intersection with YIELD signs and yield lines at each entry. Drivers entering the roundabout must yield to vehicles already in the circle.
concepts.tip: Traffic already in the circle has the right of way.

concepts.definition: When an emergency vehicle uses a siren or flashing red or red and blue lights, pull over to the curb or side of the road and stop. On a one-way street, pull toward the nearest side. Stay clear of intersections. After it passes, stay at least 500 feet behind it.
concepts.tip: Pull over, stop, and let it pass. Then keep 500 feet back.

concepts.definition: When a school bus has its red lights flashing and stop arm out, you must stop at least 10 feet from the bus. You do not need to stop if you are on the opposite side of a divided highway separated by a physical barrier, such as a grassy median, guide rail, or concrete barrier. Then slow down and drive with care.
concepts.tip: Red lights on a bus: stop 10 feet back, unless a barrier divides the highway.

source.org: PennDOT, Pennsylvania's School Bus Stopping Law (PUB 741)

concepts.definition: Treat the crossbuck like a yield sign. You must stop for flashing red lights, a lowered gate, a flagger, or a train's warning horn. Never go around a gate, and never stop on the tracks.
concepts.tip: Gates down means stop and wait. Never go around them.

points: At a four-way stop, if two vehicles arrive together, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right.
You may turn right on red after a full stop unless a sign prohibits it.
Pull over and stop for an emergency vehicle with a siren or flashing lights.
Stop at least 10 feet from a school bus with red lights flashing and its stop arm out.
Never drive around a lowered railroad gate.

compare.title: School bus with red lights flashing
rows: Coming toward the bus on an undivided road
Opposite side of a divided highway with a physical barrier
No need to stop; slow down and use caution

summary: This chapter covers the numbers that control how fast you drive, when you signal, and where you may park. Many test questions ask about one exact distance or speed, so it helps to learn them as a group.

A posted speed limit is the highest safe speed under ideal conditions, so you should drive slower in rain, snow, or heavy traffic. When no limit is posted, Pennsylvania law sets 25 mph in a residential district, 35 mph in an urban district, and 55 mph in other locations. The highest speed limit in Pennsylvania is 70 mph. In a school zone, the limit is 15 mph when the sign's lights are flashing or during the times shown on the sign.
Before you turn, signal at least 100 feet ahead if you are going less than 35 mph, and at least 300 feet ahead at 35 mph or more. Pass only where it is legal and safe, using the lane on the left.

Parking rules keep space clear for emergencies and for drivers to see. Do not park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant, within 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, within 30 feet of a stop sign, yield sign, or flashing signal at the side of the road, within 20 feet of a fire station driveway, or within 50 feet of the nearest rail at a railroad crossing. When you park next to a curb, your wheels must be no more than 12 inches from it.

concepts.term: Speed limits when none is posted
concepts.definition: 25 mph in a residential district, 35 mph in an urban district, and 55 mph in other locations. The maximum speed limit anywhere in Pennsylvania is 70 mph.
concepts.tip: 25 at home, 35 in town, 55 elsewhere.

source.org: Pennsylvania Driver's Manual (PennDOT) and Pennsylvania State Police

concepts.definition: The speed limit is 15 mph when the lights on the school zone sign are flashing or during the times shown on the sign.
concepts.tip: Flashing school sign lights: 15 mph.

concepts.definition: Use your turn signal at least 100 feet before turning if you are driving less than 35 mph. At 35 mph or more, signal at least 300 feet before turning.
concepts.tip: Under 35: 100 feet. 35 or more: 300 feet.

concepts.definition: Pass on the left, and only where lines and signs allow it and the passing lane is clear. Do not pass across a solid yellow line on your side, a double solid yellow line, or in a marked no passing zone.
concepts.tip: If you cannot see far enough ahead to pass safely, do not pass.

concepts.definition: Do not park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant, 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, 30 feet of a flashing signal, stop sign, yield sign, or other traffic control device at the side of the road, 20 feet of a fire station driveway, or 50 feet of the nearest rail at a railroad crossing.
concepts.tip: Hydrant 15, crosswalk 20, stop sign 30, railroad 50.

concepts.definition: Park as close to the curb as possible, with your wheels no more than 12 inches away. If there is no curb, pull as far off the roadway as you can.
concepts.tip: 12 inches is one foot: keep within a foot of the curb.

points: With no posted limit: 35 mph in an urban district and 55 mph in other locations.
School zone: 15 mph when the sign's lights are flashing.
Signal at least 100 feet before a turn below 35 mph, and 300 feet at 35 mph or more.
No parking within 15 feet of a fire hydrant or 30 feet of a stop sign.
Park no more than 12 inches from the curb.

compare.title: Parking distances
rows: A stop sign, yield sign, or flashing signal at the roadside
The nearest rail at a railroad crossing

summary: Safe driving means leaving yourself time and space to react. This chapter covers following distance, using your headlights, driving in bad weather and work zones, sharing the road, staying off your phone, and the Move Over law.

On dry pavement, keep at least four seconds between you and the vehicle ahead. Count from when its rear bumper passes a fixed object until your front bumper reaches the same spot. On wet roads, slow down by 5 to 10 mph and leave more space. In a work zone, double your following distance, because rear-end crashes are the most common crash there.

Pennsylvania law requires your headlights whenever your windshield wipers are on because of the weather, and daytime running lights alone do not count. Switch to low beams within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and within 300 feet of a vehicle you are following.

Keep your attention on the road. Texting while driving is against the law, and holding a phone while driving is also banned. When you come upon an emergency response area, such as a stopped police car, a tow truck, or a disabled vehicle with hazard lights, cones, or flares, move over a lane if it is safe, or slow down if you cannot.

concepts.definition: On dry pavement, keep at least four seconds behind the vehicle ahead so you can steer or brake around a hazard. Leave more time on wet or slick roads.
concepts.tip: Count one thousand one to one thousand four as you pass the same spot.

concepts.definition: Pennsylvania law requires headlights any time your wipers are in continuous or intermittent use because of the weather. Daytime running lights are not enough.
concepts.tip: Wipers on, headlights on.

concepts.definition: Use low beams when you are within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and when you are following a vehicle within 300 feet.
concepts.tip: 500 feet for oncoming, 300 feet for following.

concepts.definition: Slow down, obey the orange signs and flaggers, and double your following distance. Rear-end crashes are the most common crash in work zones.
concepts.tip: Orange signs: slow down and leave twice the space.

concepts.definition: When you approach an emergency response area, such as an emergency vehicle with flashing lights, a tow truck helping a driver, or a disabled vehicle with at least two warning signs like hazard lights, cones, or flares, move into a lane away from it if you can do so safely. If you cannot move over, slow down.
concepts.tip: Move over if you can, slow down if you cannot.

concepts.definition: Pennsylvania bans texting while driving, including reading or writing texts, instant messages, and emails. A newer law also bans holding a phone while driving; hands-free use and emergency calls are allowed.
concepts.tip: Put the phone away before you start the car.

points: Keep at least a four-second following distance on dry pavement.
On wet roads, slow down by 5 to 10 mph and leave more space.
Turn on headlights whenever your wipers are on because of the weather.
Use low beams within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle.
Double your following distance in a work zone.

summary: Pennsylvania lets new drivers build skill in steps. This chapter covers how to get a learner's permit, how much supervised practice you need before the road test, and the limits that come with a junior license.

You may apply for a learner's permit on or after your 16th birthday. To get it you pass a vision screening and the 18-question knowledge test, answering at least 15 correctly. If you fail, you may retake the test on the next business day. The permit is valid for one year, and it can be extended if you need more practice time.

If you are under 18, you must hold your permit for six months and complete at least 65 hours of supervised driving, including at least 10 hours at night and 5 hours in bad weather. A parent or guardian signs a form certifying these hours before you take the road test.

Passing the road test gives a teen a junior license. A junior driver may not drive between 11 p.m. and 5 a.m. unless an exception applies, such as work or volunteer fire company duty, or a parent, guardian, or spouse 18 or older is in the car. During the first six months, a junior driver may carry only one passenger under 18 who is not immediate family unless a parent or guardian is in the car. After six months the limit rises to three, but not for a driver who has been partly or fully responsible for a crash or convicted of a driving violation. There may never be more passengers than seat belts.

concepts.definition: You may apply on or after your 16th birthday. After you pass the knowledge test, the permit is valid for one year, with extensions for drivers who need more practice time.
concepts.tip: Age 16, valid one year.

concepts.definition: 18 multiple choice questions on traffic signs, Pennsylvania driving laws, and safe driving. You must answer at least 15 correctly. If you fail, you may retake it on the next business day.
concepts.tip: 15 of 18: you can miss only 3.

concepts.definition: Hold the permit for six months and complete at least 65 hours of behind-the-wheel practice, including at least 10 hours at night and 5 hours in bad weather. A parent or guardian certifies the hours.
concepts.tip: 6 months, 65 hours, 10 night, 5 bad weather.

concepts.definition: A junior license holder may not drive between 11 p.m. and 5 a.m. Exceptions include work, public or charitable service, and volunteer fire company duty with a signed affidavit, or riding with a parent, guardian, or spouse 18 or older.
concepts.tip: Home by 11, not out before 5.

concepts.definition: For the first six months, no more than one passenger under 18 who is not immediate family, unless a parent or guardian is in the car. After six months, up to three such passengers, but this increase does not apply to a driver who was partly or fully responsible for a crash or was convicted of a driving violation. Never more passengers than seat belts.
concepts.tip: One friend for six months, then three if your record is clean.

points: You may apply for a learner's permit on or after your 16th birthday.
Pass the knowledge test with at least 15 of 18 correct.
Under 18: hold the permit six months and log 65 hours, including 10 at night and 5 in bad weather.
Junior license: no driving from 11 p.m. to 5 a.m. unless an exception applies.
Never carry more passengers than there are seat belts.

summary: This chapter covers the laws that can cost you your license: driving under the influence, the implied consent law, the point system, and the texting ban. These rules use exact numbers, so learn them carefully.

Pennsylvania sets different blood alcohol concentration (BAC) limits for different drivers. Drivers 21 and older are considered under the influence at 0.08% or more. Drivers under 21 are considered under the influence at 0.02% or more. The limit is 0.04% when driving a commercial vehicle and 0.02% when driving a school bus or school vehicle.

By driving in Pennsylvania, you are considered to have agreed to a chemical test if police suspect you of driving under the influence. This is the implied consent law. Refusing the test automatically suspends your driving privilege for one year.

Many traffic violations add points to your driving record. When you reach 6 or more points for the first time, you must take a written Special Point Examination or attend Driver Improvement School, or your license will be suspended. Passing the Special Point Examination removes 2 points. A driver who reaches 6 points a second time must attend a departmental hearing.

concepts.definition: 0.08% or more for drivers 21 and older, 0.02% or more for drivers under 21, 0.04% or more in a commercial vehicle, and 0.02% or more in a school bus or school vehicle.
concepts.tip: Adults .08, under 21 .02, commercial .04.

concepts.definition: Driving in Pennsylvania means you have agreed to chemical testing if you are suspected of driving under the influence. Refusing the test automatically suspends your driving privilege for one year.
concepts.tip: Refuse the test, lose your license for a year.

concepts.definition: Alcohol slows your reactions and weakens your judgment and vision, even below the legal limit. Only time lowers your BAC. Coffee, a cold shower, or fresh air do not sober you up.
concepts.tip: Only time sobers you up.

concepts.definition: When your record reaches 6 or more points for the first time, you must take a written Special Point Examination or attend Driver Improvement School within the time PennDOT gives you, or your license is suspended. Passing the exam removes 2 points. A second time at 6 points leads to a departmental hearing.
concepts.tip: 6 points: test or school. Pass the test, lose 2 points.

concepts.definition: Failing to stop for a school bus with red lights flashing and stop arm out brings a $250 fine, 5 points on your record, and a 60-day license suspension.
concepts.tip: Passing a stopped school bus costs points and your license.

source.org: PennDOT, Pennsylvania's School Bus Stopping Law (PUB 741)

concepts.definition: Using a phone or other device to send, read, or write texts, instant messages, or emails while the vehicle is moving is a primary offense. Police can stop you for it alone. The fine is $50 plus costs.
concepts.tip: Police do not need another reason to stop you for texting.

points: BAC limit: 0.08% for drivers 21 and older and 0.02% for drivers under 21.
The BAC limit in a commercial vehicle is 0.04%.
Refusing a chemical test means a one-year suspension.
6 points for the first time: Special Point Examination or Driver Improvement School.
Texting while driving is a primary offense.
